**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Previously system reserved cgroup could not be declared if `--reserved-cpus` option was used. Now it's allowed, and the cpuset defined with `--reserved-cpus` will be assigned to the system reserved cgroup if `--enforce-node-allocatable=system-reserved`.

So, in order to let system services (assigned to cpuset /foobar.slice on a systemd system) on CPUs 4 and 5, you could run kubelet with

    kubelet --reserved-cpus=4,5 \
            --enforce-node-allocatable=system-reserved \
            --system-reserved-cgroup=foobar

@jianzzha The current docs say:

> reserved-cpus is meant to define an explicit CPU set for OS system daemons and kubernetes system daemons. This option is added in 1.17 release. reserved-cpus is for systems that do not intent to define separate top level cgroups for OS system daemons and kubernetes system daemons with regard to cpuset resource.

The idea in this PR is to let systems define the top-level cgroup for OS system daemons and automatically restrict the cpuset there according to reserved-cpus setting. In effect the last sentence above would be replaced something like this:

> You can optionally use reserved-cpus with a system cgroup. In this configuration the OS system daemons will be restricted to run only on cpus present in the reserved-cpus cpuset.

It is actually a good question whether or not the same semantics should follow for `kube-reserved` cgroup, too. We could let the `--kube-reserved-cgroup` be restricted to the reserved-cpus cpuset, if both are present on the command line, in exactly the same way as this PR proposes for the `system-reserved` cgroup. What do you think?

potential challenge of having a cpuset cgroup for system-reserved and enforcing it:
all systemd service cgroup need to be under this parent cgroup.  Since some of them starts before kubelet and have already have their individual cpuset.cpus set;  when kubelet starts and enforce this on the parent setting, it needs to reset each of the individual service unit'  cpuset.cpus first. Have you tested your code and see if this actually happens?

I did a quick test and yes my concern is valid - if there is already other system service unit under this system-reserved-cgroup, the simple update on this system-reserved-cgroup will not work.

To make it work, update all pre-existing systemd service  under the cpuset cgroup is necessary. However there might be danger of doing that - what if some service unit has its own cpuset setting for whatever purpose that it wants to keep.

For now We did have a workaround as described in  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/85764

@jianzzha If I understand correctly, you mean a scenario like this:
```
└─system.slice
  ├─foobar.service
  │ └─1019 /sbin/foobar
```
Here `foobar.service` would have been set by systemd to have (for example) a cpuset of `0-5`, and then kubelet would try to set the `system.slice` cpuset to be (for example) `4-6` and fail because the top-level cpuset needs to include the cpus in all the leaf cpusets.

I think the right solution here would be to error out with a good error message: the two configuration sources (systemd and kubelet) are conflicting. The problem is that in order for the system to function as needed, the requested system-reserved cpuset cannot be used, and the administrator needs to find out what's the reason for that and how it should be solved.

Hey @ipuustin, sorry for the *long* delay on getting back to you on this.

After reading through the comments and thinking about this for a while, I have the following comments / suggestions:

1) It feels a bit strange to arbitrarily decide that the `--reserved-cpus` flag should *only* be linked  to `system-reserved` CPUs  such that setting `--enforce-node-allocatable=system-reserved` will set the `cpuset` for these CPUs on the `system-reserved-cgroup`.

2) In the same vein, it  would be just as strange to arbitrarily decide that the `--reserved-cpus` flag should *only* be linked  to `kube-reserved` CPUs  such that setting `--enforce-node-allocatable=kube-reserved` will set the `cpuset` for these CPUs on the `kube-reserved-cgroup`.

3) It feels equally as strange to arbitrarily decide that combining them (as you have done in your most recent patch) to say that `--reserved-cpus`  links to both `system-reserved` *and* `kube-reserved` such that the same `cpuset` will be set up for both of them if specified as part of `--enforce-node-allocatable`.

As such, I feel like the only way to deal with this properly would be to introduce separate `--system-reserved-cpus` and `--kube-reserved-cpus` (or something similar) such that:

1) A user has *not* specified `--reserved-cpus` (which, as the documentation states, always takes precedence over any kube-reserved or kube-reserved settings). 
2) The number of CPUs listed in `--system-reserved-cpus` and `--kube-reserved-cpus` *matches* the CPU count specified in `system-reserved` and `kube-reserved` respectively.

I still think having introduced `--reserved-cpus` on its own is useful for cases where the sysadmin really wants to manage these CPUs himself (and not use system-reserved or kube-reserved at all). But trying to arbitrarily map `--reserved-cpus` onto either `system-reserved`, `kube-reserved` (or both )doesn't fell like a good approach.

/cc @derekwaynecarr

for his thoughts

Thanks @klueska for your comments!

I think the main point of this effort is automation of the cgroup cpuset settings. I believe that currently people are using `--reserved-cpus=` cpuset so that they assign the system services (and kube services) to that cpuset manually (to keep the guaranteed pods allocated to free cpus). The point of this PR is to automate the effort.

Adding new command line options (`--system-reserved-cpus` and `--kube-reserved-cpus`) definitely helps to achieve three goals:
 1. Being able to allocate a separate cpuset to kube services. I can think of a situation where the user might want to run those services on a separate cpuset than the system daemons, especially if there is some negative interaction between them.
 2. There is no need to touch the semantics of the existing command line options.
 3. Explicit is better than implicit. 

However, the problems I see are:
 1. Unclear semantics for `--enforce-node-allocatable=`. Is it needed for the new options to take effect or not? If not, why does it work differently?
 2. Confusion with the existing `--reserved-cpus=` option. In a way, this will mean that `--reserved-cpus=` option just "takes away" cpus for later manual assignment by the user, while `--system-reserved-cpus=` takes them away and assigns them right away to the system cgroup. A natural question is to ask what happens if `--reserved-cpus=` is set at the same time as `--system-reserved-cgroup=`, and why doesn't that work.
 2. Adding more kubelet options slowly leads to an combinatoric explosion -- we need to understand the semantics of all combinations (whether they are allowed and what do they mean) and possibly "recommend" some settings for various use cases.

I plan to go forward with this by implementing your suggestion to try it out in practice. It's easier to discuss the concepts with the code,

issue_context.title: processes from /system.slice using cores assigned to guaranteed Pods when --cpu-manager-policy=static is set
issue_context.body:
**What happened**:

Following is the configuration for kubelet to enable the --cpu-manager-policy=static feature.

**_--cpu-manager-policy=static --system-reserved=cpu=10,memory=10Gi --system-reserved-cgroup=/system.slice._**

There is no separate cgroup for the kubelet and hence --kube-reserved is not used.

./user.slice
./system.slice
./system.slice/system-getty.slice

PSR field of "ps -eLF " command on the host shows that processes from /system.slice are using cores assigned to the Application Pods  which are guaranteed and integer cores assigned.

Here is /var/lib/kubelet/cpu_manager_state which shows that  this Pod is assigned 8-11 and 32 - 35

{"policyName":"static","defaultCpuSet":"0-7,12-31,36-47","entries":{"f7cc858318f3a84d9cbd340e058126379292f09578ca362680e3a350c8edad63":"8-11,32-35"},"checksum":462128154}

on the Host,
ps -eLF | awk '{print $9 " " $13 " " $14 " " $2 " " $3}' | sort | grep -i glusterfs
8 /usr/sbin/glusterfs --log-level=ERROR 8870 1

Here 8 is the core ,PID 8870 and PPID is 1. Following command shows that cgroup of the PID 8870 is /system.slice

$ cat /proc/8870/cgroup
11:hugetlb:/
10:freezer:/
9:blkio:/system.slice/run-rf63a79fe920945f497cdb8ed37874e36.scope
8:memory:/system.slice/run-rf63a79fe920945f497cdb8ed37874e36.scope
7:pids:/system.slice/run-rf63a79fe920945f497cdb8ed37874e36.scope
6:cpuset:/
5:net_cls,net_prio:/
4:perf_event:/
3:cpu,cpuacct:/system.slice/run-rf63a79fe920945f497cdb8ed37874e36.scope
2:devices:/system.slice/run-rf63a79fe920945f497cdb8ed37874e36.scope
1:name=systemd:/system.slice/run-rf63a79fe920945f497cdb8ed37874e36.scope

Similarly there are other processes from the /system.slice like docker daemon etc also using the cores assigned to this Pod.

**What you expected to happen**:

No system process from /system.slice should be scheduled on the cores assigned to this guaranteed Pod having integer CPU  

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.15.3
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):

It seems to me that the `cpuset` cgroup of the pid 8870 you mention is just `/` instead of `/system.slice`:

```
6:cpuset:/
```

The `cpuset` cgroup controls the "integer" cpus on which the process executes.

I looked a bit further and it seems that the 10-core request is converted into cpu shares:

```
Jan 15 15:27:24 test kubelet[46360]: I0115 15:27:24.337944   46360 node_container_manager_linux.go:105] Enforcing System reserved on cgroup "/system.slice" with limits: map[cpu:{i:{value:10 scale:0} d:{Dec:<nil>} s:10 Format:DecimalSI}]
Jan 15 15:27:24 test kubelet[46360]: I0115 15:27:24.337977   46360 node_container_manager_linux.go:134] Enforcing limits on cgroup ["system"] with 824649638272 cpu shares, 0 bytes of memory, and 0 processes
```

Especially https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/types.go#L25, which is used to set the cgroup limit, doesn't have a field for integer CPU requests. Also, container manager only knows that "10" cpus are reserved, but it's not told which ones those are.

Thanks.

I have a PR which should help with your problem here by automating the cpuset resource setting to system-reserved cgroup: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/87452

You can set a cpuset on a cgroup by writing the `cpuset.cpus` file. The exact way to do it depends on your cgroup setup but something like this might work:

    # echo "1-4" > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset/system.slice/cpuset.cpus

Note that if you are reducing the cpuset, you need to first set it to all subdirectories (the parent cgroup can't have a smaller cpuset than the child cgroup). Otherwise you will get "permission denied" errors. The docs are here: https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/cgroup-v1/cpusets.txt

@subrnath @ipuustin --reserved-cpus option is meant to be used with either isolcpu kargs or systemd CPUAffinity control. Using systemd CPUAffinity as an example, in /etc/systemd/system.conf, specify CPUAffinity=0 1 2 3; reboot the machine to make sure systemd take it; then for kubelet specify --reserved-cpus=0-3. see if this works for you, at least as a workaround.

As @ipuustin mentioned, enable cpuset cgroup setting might be another way to solve this - need to check if it is realistic - we will discuss that in the other PR.

@jianzzha @ipuustin  I read the discussion above, and try to understand your statement/conclusion:
If we just need to do CPU isolation in K8S, then we only need to set "--reserved-cpus" in kubelet
and configure "CPUAffinity" in "/etc/systemd/system.conf" should be enough?
No other parameter is needed? 
"--system-reserved", "--system-reserved-cgroup", "--kube-reserved" and "--kube-reserved-cgroup"can be skipped as they do nothing about CPU isolation. right?

"--reserved-cpus" can avoid Guaranteed Pods to be landed on given cpuset, and  "CPUAffinity" can let all systemd managed process to stay the given cpuset.
